messages.subject: rqgam.check with Tweedie
parts:
Hello all,

I'd like to know what folks think of the attached randomized quantile residuals vs linear predictor plot. I thought rqgam.check() was supposed to randomize out the artifacts caused by the discrete nature of the data, but plainly in the plot, it appears as though only the zeros have gotten that treatment. This does not occur in negative binomial rq plots of the same data, so is this just because tweedie expects continuous data ergo qres.tweedie() doesn't apply the randomization, whereas negative binomial expects discrete? Or is this a sign tweedie does not fit the data? The tweedie rq plots for all of my species groups look like this (more or less). Despite the artifacts, it doesn't appear that there is much heterogeneity in the variance, so I'm thinking Tweedie isn't necessarily a bad fit.

I have a secondary question too. On occasion I am getting negative R.sq for negative binomial models, whereas the % deviance explained is perfectly reasonable (~30%). In tweedie models of the same data, all of a sudden this is not an issue and R.sq is a reasonable value close to %dev. Same data, same covariates, so it doesn't seem as though the models are overparameterized, which i know can be a cause of negative adjusted R.sq. The interesting thing is that nb() is preferable to tw() on the basis of AIC, so i'd use it, except that the negative R.sq is giving me pause. I would use tweedie, except for the aforementioned question about the rq plots. 

Thanks for all your help,
Kevin

Hi Kevin, hi listfolk,

A couple of things here:

- running rqgam.check multiple times should yield different plots due to
the randomisation, check that this happens for you (it does for me with
nb(), tw() and Tweedie() response families). If it doesn't check you
have the latest dsm and statmod packages. If you're still not getting
anywhere please do send me an example off-list and I'll take a look.

- the aim of the residuals vs linear predictor plot is to check for
constant variance. If there is-non constant variance the plot will look
more like a cone (or triangle or trumpet?) -- widening or narrowing left
to right. The aim of the using rq or pit residuals is to ensure that
artefacts of the data (like only a few unique counts being observed)
don’t get in the way of your interpretation of the plot.

- finally, regarding R^2. I don’t consider R^2 to be a useful measure of
model fit. A concise and compelling argument against it is given in the
course notes from Cosma Shalizi given here:
http://www.stat.cmu.edu/~cshalizi/mreg/15/lectures/10/lecture-10.pdf so
I won’t reiterate here.

Hope this is helpful!

cheers,
—dave
